newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Maradona manager freed from jail, says he was framed.
newsitem.headline: Maradona manager freed from jail, says he was framed.

text.p: Argentine soccer star Diego Maradona's manager, Guillermo Coppola, walked free from jail on Tuesday after three months and declared the drug charges against him were a fabrication.
"I was framed," he told TV interviewer Mauro Viale, who has devoted his daily programme entirely to the case from its start. "Everything is a big lie."

Judge Carlos Liporaci ruled there was insufficient evidence to keep Coppola behind bars, where he had been since October when police raided his luxury Buenos Aires apartment and seized a pound (400 g) of cocaine hidden in a vase.

"My conscience is clear", said Coppola, who maintains the drugs were planted. Although we was released from jail, he is still under investigation on charges of possessing drugs and supplying cocaine at a party at his home. He will have to report to the judge every 30 days.
His once-permanent tan faded, Coppola was driven away from prison in a black BMW limousine, which pushed through a crowd of reporters outside a Buenos Aires police station.
But by the evening his good looks were back and, although he said he felt like killing himself when he was thrown into jail, Coppola told Viale: "I feel in one piece, I feel alright, I feel strong."

Local television reported Maradona had rented a house at the beach resort of Mar del Plata to welcome his manager and close friend, whose arrest sparked massive media interest and catapulted the key witnesses in the case to stardom.

Revelling in the limelight, government witnesses Samantha Farjat and Natalia de Negri became among the best-known women in Argentina as they poured out sordid details of celebrity drug-taking and sex and swapped contradictory accusations.
Farjat's racy revelations were recorded by a local singer and "The Samantha Rap" raced up pop music charts propelled by the catchy chorus "Samantha keeps hard at it all night."

Farjat alleged police blackmailed her to plant drugs on another investigation target -- former Argentina national soccer team player Alberto Tarantini. He was freed and a top judge's aide and three undercover policemen were arrested.

The Coppola case has been an embarrassment for President Carlos Menem, who backs the death penalty for drug smugglers. Coppola was a friend of his late son, Carlitos, and of his private secretary, Ramon Hernandez.
